newsitem.title: CHINA: China should boost net grain imports - experts.
newsitem.headline: China should boost net grain imports - experts.

text.p: China should raise its net grain imports to cover anticipated shortfalls in the longer term while expanding sales of high value-added farm products to earn foreign currency, Chinese experts said on Wednesday.

"Appropriately lowering the degree of self-sufficiency and raising grain imports would help China's agriculture to shape its own characteristics and strengths," a top research body said in a recent report.

The report, titled "Agriculture and Development -- Strategic Research on China's Grain and Agriculture Development in the 21st Century", was released by a research group under the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

"We should learn to take advantage of the international market to develop our own agriculture," said Hu Angang, a senior researcher with the National Conditions Analysis and Research Group who helped to compile the report.
China should raise its net grain imports to 10 percent of annual consumption by the year 2020 from the current two percent, Hu said in a telephone interview.
The government has set an import ceiling of five percent.
China imported 12 million tonnes of grain in 1996, down 42 percent from the previous year, official figures showed.
"China could make itself fully self-sufficient, but the cost would be too high," Hu said.
Instead of exporting high-priced grains, China should boost sales of value-added farm products including aquatic products, vegetables and fruits to earn foreign currency, he said.
China's grains and oil products have lost their competitive edge against foreign products on international markets because of rising domestic output costs, said the research report.
The average wholesale price of domestic rice, wheat and corn was 21 percent higher than average international prices in 1996, said the report made available to Reuters.
Grain experts attributed the high costs to increases in state grain purchase prices and the low quality of fertiliser, which forced farmers to use more.
"China's agricultural development will face severe difficulties and challenges in the 21st century," the report said.
It forecast China's grain shortfall would hit 50 million tonnes by the year 2030 with total consumption at 700 million.
"China should consider grain imports at appropriate levels," said Xin Naiquan, head of the Science and Technology Bureau of the China Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
"It is impossble for China to cover its grain shortfalls without importing from the international market," Xin said.
It would be difficult for China to balance grain consumption and supply in the next 30 years mainly due to its growing population, he said.
China's polulation, now at about 1.2 billion, is expected to hit 1.6 billion by 2030, Xin said.
However, China was unlikely to import substantial amounts of grains in the long term because of the official desire for self-sufficiency, experts said.
"The market could not be fully open (to foreign imports). We need appropriate protection," Hu said.
High imports would hurt farmers and raise international prices, the report said. Also, China lacks transport and port facilities to handle large shipments.

China should rely mainly on improved farm technology to boost per hectare output because yields on about 66 percent of its arable land were relatively low, leaving room for a large hike in production, he said.
China has reported two consecutive record grain harvests of 465 million tonnes in 1995 and 490 million tonnes last year, although the figures also include items such as beans and tubers.
